posts.quote: THE NEW NEIGHBOR ASKED IF I'M ONE OF THOSE HORSES THAT BITES. I SAID I'M ONE OF THOSE HORSES THAT REMEMBERS.
posts.first: Red has never bitten anyone. She has, however, stood on a boot for six minutes until an apology was offered in full. I keep a spare pair in the truck for that reason. She's very fair. She just keeps a better record than the rest of us do.

Text at the top reads: The new neighbor asked if I'm one of those horses that bites. I said I'm one of those horses that remembers.
posts.caption: The new boarder's husband came to drop off a bucket and stayed at the gate for ten minutes, studying Red like a firework he'd been told was probably fine. I said she's a sweetheart. Red lifted one hoof about an inch and he took two steps back. He has brought the bucket to the fence line ever since. Last Saturday he left a peppermint on the post and walked away briskly. She ate it with her eyes on him the whole time. It's the most polite arrangement I've ever seen between two adults. They've never touched, and I'd call them close.

posts.first: I bought a third net last night. He watched me hang it from the aisle rafter with the expression of a pony who has already read the instructions. I went to bed feeling optimistic. I'll be out there at six to see how that feeling holds up.

posts.caption: The hay net used to be a fifteen minute project. Last month the vet said Pudding could stand to lose a little around the middle, so I switched to the net with the small holes. By the next morning he had worked out the knot. The diet is a work in progress. The knot has been solved.

posts.quote: The vet called it a routine visit. In eleven years, that phrase has never once appeared on an invoice.
posts.first: I've kept every vet invoice in a folder since the first year, mostly so I can look at them in the same order and feel nothing. The folder is thicker than the horse's registration papers. The horse, for his part, has never once asked what anything costs.

posts.quote: I found my first gray hair this morning. She called it distinguished and then spent ten minutes trying to cover it with my forelock. We've agreed to blame the light.
posts.first: Mine showed up the year she turned three. I told her it was from stress and she took that personally. She still turns her head when I part my hair in the barn mirror, like she's checking my work. I leave the part where it is.

posts.caption: I spotted it while braiding her forelock this morning, one pale hair right at the root, and I made the mistake of calling it distinguished. The Diva went very still. She looked at the tack room mirror, then at me, then at the mirror again. I spent ten minutes rearranging her forelock until it fell over the spot just so. She checked it twice and approved. I have about a dozen of my own, mostly from her, and she never offered to hide any of them. The mirror has since been moved. She picked the wall.

posts.quote: The kid who rode me today is eleven and called me a legend. I've mostly stood in this field since 2009. I'll accept the title anyway.
posts.first: He was twenty-four when I got him and the barn manager called him a short-term project. That was two winters ago. He has taught six kids to post the trot and one adult to breathe. I haven't updated the paperwork. He knows.

posts.caption: A girl from the lesson program rode the old gelding for the first time yesterday, a quiet eleven-year-old in a helmet two sizes too big. They walked three laps of the arena at a speed I'd call geological. He never lifted his feet higher than necessary. When she got off she patted his neck and said, very seriously, that he was a legend. He lifted his head and blinked at her. I have never seen him do either of those things for an adult. She went home with a story, and he went back to the fence standing a little taller.

posts.quote: THE FORECAST SAYS FLURRIES BY NOON. / I'VE ALREADY CANCELLED MY MORNING.
posts.first: Her first winter here I tried to turn her out in light snow. She walked to the gate, looked at the sky, looked at me, and walked back. We've had the same conversation every storm since. I bring the water to her now and she thanks me by not moving.

posts.caption: The first flurries are due at noon and I already know where I'll find the Homebody. She'll be in the back corner of her stall with the cat on her back, a fresh flake of hay and the door open just a crack. I stopped fighting this around her second winter. I put out two buckets, she picks the warm one, and I carry water at four. The weather app says one inch. She says nothing, because she's asleep. Somehow she is still the only one in the barn who is right about every storm.
